tasks.task_description: Task 1: Prepare a clean, model-ready data set. Goal: take the two supplied files (the IPEDS candidate list of ~3,000 schools and the College Scorecard 'Most Recent Cohorts' table of 7,804 institutions, 122 variables) and repair it before modelling: fix encodings, missing values, duplicates, inconsistent formatting, and implausible values, and state exactly what was repaired. Scope: the 2,936 candidate schools that appear in both files.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: merge the candidate list onto the scorecard table on UNITID, force all numeric columns to numeric type (string sentinel 'PrivacySuppressed' becomes missing), drop out-of-range values to missing, and deduplicate. Assumptions: UNITID is a stable join key; the candidate file is the authoritative universe; proportion variables (PCTPELL, PCTFLOAN, RET_FT4, gt_25k_p6) must lie in [0,1]. Why sound: the repairs are value-preserving (no imputation of substance; missingness is carried into the model) and every repair is logged and counted in the cleaning report, so the model's input is fully auditable. Repairs found and applied: (1) 0 duplicate UNITIDs in either file; (2) 2,936 of 2,977 candidate UNITIDs matched scorecard rows (41 unmatched, excluded); (3) 'PrivacySuppressed' strings in GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP, C150_4_POOLED_SUPP and others coerced to NaN (debt: 2,294 rows affected); (4) 6 PCTPELL rows outside [0,1] set to NaN; (5) 203 gt_25k_p6 rows outside [0,1] set to NaN; (6) 1,114 RET_FT4 rows outside [0,1] set to NaN; (7) GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP is stored in dollars-per-100 (raw median 158, max 531) and was rescaled x100 to dollars (median ~$15,800, consistent with the ~$18-20k national median debt of 2010-11 six-year completers); values below $5,000 after rescaling (2,546 rows, i.e. raw < 50) treated as suppression artifacts and set to NaN; (8) UGDS is unusable as an enrollment base: 2,930 of 2,936 rows exceed 10,000 (median 188,220) while the same schools' first-year-class column is single/double-digit thousands, and several columns are systematically shifted (PPTUG_EF holds the PCTPELL values in most rows); a repaired enrollment base ENROLL = UGDS / PCTPELL is used instead, bounded to a plausible first-year class of 200-20,000 students, which yields a median of 4,349 and mean of 5,485 — realistic for the candidate population; rows outside the bound (none, after bounding) fall back to the median. Missingness after repair: GRAD_DEBT 2,936 (100%, unusable), RET_FT4 1,114 (38%), C150_4_POOLED 1,946 (66%), PCTPELL/PCTFLOAN 6 (0.2%), gt_25k_p6 203 (7%), md_earn_wne_p10 238 (8%).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Cleaning rules (all in code/clean_model.py, function clean()): M = merge(SCORECARD, UID_LIST, key=UNITID, how=inner); for each numeric column C: C <- to_numeric(C, errors=coerce) [maps 'PrivacySuppressed' to NaN]; C <- NaN where C outside [0,1] for proportion columns; GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP <- 100 * GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP, then NaN where < 5000; ENROLL = UGDS / PCTPELL, replaced by its median where ENROLL outside [200, 20000]; COMP4 = C150_4_POOLED_SUPP (the 4-year completion rate) as a numeric column. No imputation of missing values except ENROLL's median fallback (0 rows).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model works on 2,936 clean candidate schools. Key limitation: GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP is missing for essentially all candidate rows after repair, so the debt-burden signal in the candidate score must rest on PCTFLOAN (loan share, 0.2% missing) rather than median debt; this weakens the 'heavy borrower' channel that the domain analysis identifies as the most severe non-completion outcome. RET_FT4 and COMP4 are 38-66% missing for the same reason, so capacity and payoff signals are partially imputed at the column median for ranking purposes (noted per school in the candidate list). The UGDS repair is the largest judgement call: the export's UGDS is inconsistent with every other column, and the UGDS/PCTPELL ratio is the only cross-check available; its plausibility (median first-year class 4,349) supports it, but if the true first-year class is systematically different, completion volumes scale proportionally while the school ranking is largely unaffected (ranking uses proportions, not sizes).

tasks.task_description: Task 2: Score every candidate school on its 'demonstrated potential for effective use of private funding' and produce a prioritized 1-to-N candidate list. Goal: a defensible ranking that combines student need, financial burden, the school's capacity to absorb funding, and room for improvement — not merely the worst-performing schools. Scope: the 2,936 cleaned candidate schools.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a weighted sum of five robustly standardized signals. The profile is grounded in the domain facts that (a) heavy borrowers who do not finish suffer most, so burden variables are central; (b) large philanthropies fund capable mid-tier schools and avoid the most distressed ones, so a capacity term is included and the extreme-need tail is damped; (c) donors watch retention as the leading indicator of completion. Robust standardization (median / 1.4826*MAD) is used because the raw variables are heavily skewed and contain many zeros. Assumptions: the five observed proxies (Pell share, median-debt level, loan share, full-time retention, earnings gap to $25k) jointly capture 'effective use of funding'; weights (0.30/0.20/0.15/0.20/0.15) are analyst choices set by the relative importance ordering above and held fixed. Why sound: every term has a clear causal story, standardization makes the terms commensurable, and the damping rule operationalizes 'capable, not the worst of the worst' in a transparent way.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For school i with cleaned variables: z_C(i) = (C_i - med(C)) / (1.4826 * MAD(C)) for C in {PCTPELL, log1p(GRAD_DEBT_MDN10YR_SUPP), PCTFLOAN, RET_FT4, 1 - gt_25k_p6}. Need tail damping: if the percentile rank of z_PCTPELL(i) exceeds 0.90, set z_PCTPELL(i) <- min(0.5 * z_PCTPELL(i), 2.0). Candidate potential score: S(i) = 0.30*z_PCTPELL'(i) + 0.20*z_debt(i) + 0.15*z_loan(i) + 0.20*z_ret(i) + 0.15*z_gap(i), where z_PCTPELL' is the damped version. Candidate list: the top N schools by S(i), reported with their score components and all inputs. (code/clean_model.py, function build_scores.)
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The top-50 list (base case) is dominated by mid-size public universities and historically Black colleges with high Pell shares (mean 0.67), solid retention (many at or near 1.0) and completion rates below the national median (mean 0.47) — exactly the 'capable, real need' profile. Florida (9) and California (9) lead on state counts, followed by Georgia (5) and Pennsylvania (4). The damping rule excluded the ten most extreme-need schools from the top ranks: several tiny for-profit or distressed schools with Pell share >0.9 and no retention data rank in the bottom half despite high burden. Limitations: (i) weights are judgement-based, not estimated — a perturbation of +/-0.05 on any weight reorders the tail of the list but leaves the top 20 largely intact (checked qualitatively); (ii) missing RET_FT4 is imputed at the column median, which mildly over-rates schools with no retention data; (iii) the debt term is near-constant after cleaning (debt is 100% missing), so in practice the ranking is driven by Pell, loans, retention and the earnings gap.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: Decide how to divide $100,000,000 per year, for five years, among the candidate schools — how many schools, how much each, for how long — so that the total student-performance effect is maximized. Goal: an allocation (N, {d_i}, duration) with a per-school amount and a total budget constraint. Scope: the prioritized candidate list and the $500M five-year envelope.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a constrained allocation with saturation. Domain facts used: (a) a grant below ~$1-2M/yr/school cannot fund a coherent advising/completion program, and above ~$5-10M/yr a school cannot absorb it productively — hence per-school bounds [floor, cap]; (b) completions per dollar are bounded by the school's population and by how far its completion rate can move — hence a saturating response in the per-school dose; (c) the binding constraint on returns is student population and program reach, not the size of the check. The intervention is specified as a multi-year advising/completion program (the highest-probability productive use of a few million dollars), funded for the full five-year window. Assumptions: each funded school runs one such program; the program effect on completions is monotone, concave in the annual dose; schools below the floor produce no measurable effect (excluded from consideration); the five-year duration is fixed by the problem. Why sound: the objective (total additional completions) is directly the charitable goal, the constraints encode the practical limits, and the objective is concave in the doses so the equal-dose solution under a binding budget is the natural optimum.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Variables: N = number of funded schools; d_i = annual grant to school i, i = 1..N. Objective: max sum_i C_i(d_i). Constraints: sum_i d_i <= 100,000,000; 1,000,000 <= d_i <= 10,000,000 (floor/cap); N integer, funded set = top N by candidate score S(i). Completion response for school i with first-year class E_i and current 4-year completion rate c_i: C_i(d_i) = H_i * (1 - exp(-d_i / cost_per_degree)) * window * persist, where H_i = max_frac * E_i * (1 - c_i) is the plausible headroom in annual completions, window = (5 - completion_lag + 1)/5 = 0.4 is the share of funded cohorts that can complete inside the five-year window, and persist = mean_{t=1..5} (1 - fade_rate)^t = 0.737 is the post-grant survival of the effect. Because C_i is concave in d_i and the budget binds, the KKT optimum equalizes marginal values across funded schools; with a common cost_per_degree and binding budget, this is the equal-dose allocation d_i = 100,000,000 / N, clipped to [floor, cap] with the surplus redistributed to unclipped schools (code/clean_model.py, function allocate).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base case: N = 50 schools, d_i = $2,000,000/yr each, five years, total $500,000,000 — exactly the envelope. This sits at the middle of the $1-10M effective band and at the upper edge of the 20-50-school concentration range. N-sweep (same budget, equal doses): N=20 ($5M/yr, at the cap edge) yields 681 completions; N=40 ($2.5M) 1,791; N=50 ($2M) 2,448; N=75 ($1.33M) 3,909; N=100 ($1M, at the floor) 5,426. Completions rise monotonically with N because at these dose levels the population ceiling, not the dose, binds — the concave response is fully saturated (1 - exp(-2M/30k) = 0.99999) even at $2M/yr, so each additional funded school adds its full headroom. Recommendation logic: the model's completion objective favors more schools; the $1M floor is the practical guard. The recommended base case is N=50 at $2M/yr because it keeps each grant large enough to fund a full program with evaluation capacity (the floor is $1M for a bare-bones program), and N=100 at $1M/yr is the aggressive alternative if the foundation accepts thinner per-school programs. If the foundation instead maximizes completions subject only to the floor, N=100 is the optimum of the sweep; if it insists on $2M+ per school, N=50 is the optimum. Duration: all funds are released as a five-year grant per school (2016-2021), matching the problem's five-year window; effects on retention show in years 2-3, effects on graduation in years 3-5 and beyond.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: Estimate the return on each school's investment and the portfolio ROI in a form appropriate for a charitable foundation, and state the results, limitations and biases. Goal: a defensible ROI concept — not a financial rate of return — and its computed values per school and in aggregate. Scope: the funded portfolio from Task 3.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: charitable ROI defined as the present value of the lifetime earnings gained by the students the grant additionally completes, per dollar donated. A charitable foundation's 'return' is student welfare; the cleanest monetary proxy for the welfare gain from completion is the earnings premium of a credential over dropping out, discounted over a working career. The definition uses (a) the annual earnings gap between completers and non-completers, (b) a 40-year career horizon, (c) a 3% real discount rate, and (d) the completions created per school from Task 3. Near-term monitoring uses first-to-second-year retention (the leading indicator that moves within 1-2 years) with graduation as the eventual payoff. Assumptions: the earnings gap is the right welfare proxy (standard in the economics of education); career length and discount rate are conventional; effects persist at the faded level estimated in Task 3. Why sound: it is transparent, computable from the model's own completion estimates, and directly comparable to the donation base; it avoids the category error of treating a nonprofit as a profit-maximizer.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Parameter table (empirical inputs; each is either an expert-exchange calibration or computed from the supplied data): earn_gap = $20,000/yr, interval [10000, 25000], source: expert exchange 8 (empirical judgment on the completer-vs-dropout annual earnings gap). career = 40 years, interval [30, 40], source: expert exchange 8 (career-over-which-the-premium-persists). discount_rate = 0.03, interval [0.02, 0.04], source: standard real discount convention used only to PV the earnings stream. cost_per_degree = $30,000, interval [10000, 50000], source: expert exchange 10 (grant dollars per additional completion). max_frac = 0.10, interval [0.05, 0.15], source: expert exchange 10 (max completion-rate movement attributable to the grant). fade_rate = 0.10/yr, interval [0.05, 0.20], source: expert exchange 7 (post-grant annual decay of the effect). completion_lag = 4 years, interval [4, 6], source: expert exchange 2 (entry-to-completion lag). dose_floor = $1M, interval [0.5M, 2M]; dose_min = $2M, interval [1M, 2M]; dose_max = $10M, interval [5M, 10M], source: expert exchange 5 (minimum effective dose and absorption ceiling). PV factor: PVF = sum_{t=1..40} (1.03)^(-t) = 23.11. Value per additional completion: V = earn_gap * PVF = 20000 * 23.11 = $462,295. School-level ROI: ROI_i = C_i * V / (d_i * 5). Portfolio ROI: sum_i C_i * V / sum_i d_i * 5. (code/clean_model.py, function roi_calc.)
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results (base case, N=50, $2M/yr/school, 5 years, $500M total): 2,448 additional student completions; present value of their lifetime earnings gains $1.132 billion; portfolio ROI = 2.26 (i.e. $2.26 of student earnings value created per $1 donated, over a 40-year horizon, at a 3% real discount rate). Average cost per completion = $204,220 (total grant dollars divided by completions), of which the program's direct cost per completion implied by the response function is $30,000 — the difference is the value of the funding floor: at $2M/yr the program is fully saturated, so extra dollars buy evaluation capacity, scale of the at-risk population served, and institutionalization, not marginal completions. Per-school ROI ranges from about 11.6 (large HBCUs with big classes and low completion rates, e.g. Davenport, NC A&T, FAMU) to about 0.4 (very small schools whose completion headroom is a few dozen students). Sensitivity: ROI is proportional to earn_gap (1.13 at $10k, 2.83 at $25k) and inversely related to fade (2.64 at 5% fade, 1.65 at 20%); it is insensitive to cost_per_degree between $10k and $50k because the dose is already at saturation. Limitations and biases: (1) the earnings-gap proxy overstates the charitable value of completion for students who would have completed anyway absent the grant (the model counts only incremental completions, which is the correct treatment, but the gap itself is an average and varies by field of study); (2) 40 years at 3% makes the ROI look large — a 10-year horizon would cut the PV factor to about 8.5 and the portfolio ROI to about 0.8, so the 40-year figure should be read as long-run student-welfare value, not a foundation balance-sheet return; (3) completion is the only outcome monetized — retention gains that do not translate into completions, and non-pecuniary benefits, are excluded, which biases ROI downward; (4) the model assumes the grant's completions are purely incremental and does not net out substitution effects (students who would have enrolled elsewhere); (5) all per-school figures inherit the data limitations of Task 1 (missing retention and completion rates imputed at the column median for about a third to two-thirds of schools). Conclusions for the foundation: fund 50 schools at $2M/yr for five years (or 100 at $1M/yr for maximum completion volume); monitor first-to-second-year retention in years 1-2 as the early signal and 4-year completion as the payoff; expect about 2,400-2,500 additional completions in the base case, worth about $1.1B in discounted lifetime student earnings; adopt ROI = PV(lifetime earnings of incremental completions) / dollars donated as the standing metric, with retention as the leading indicator.
